newsitem.title: GERMANY: Iran opposition denounce Bonn deputy's Tehran trip.
newsitem.headline: Iran opposition denounce Bonn deputy's Tehran trip.

text.p: Iran's exiled resistance movement condemned on Monday a weekend visit to Tehran by maverick German politician Juergen Moellemann, saying the visit condoned Iran's "terrorism abroad" and "suppression at home".

The National Council of Resistance (NCR) of Iran, which opposes the Tehran government, denounced the liberal Free Democrat parliamentarian and former economics minister, saying his actions flouted European Union policy on Iran.

"Such visits...only encourage the mullahs' religious terrorist dictatorship and embolden it to continue suppression at home and export of terrorism abroad," said a statement from the mujahideen resistance group's leader, Massoud Radjavi.
Moellemann was not immediately available for comment.

An Iranian newspaper, the Tehran Times, reported that the politician had during his visit called for a restoration of diplomatic and economic ties with Germany, severed after a Berlin court concluded Tehran had ordered political killings.
The German Foreign Ministry said Moelleman, who is regarded as something of a maverick in Bonn, had not been on a ministry assignment but had gone to Tehran on his own iniative.
The Tehran Times English-language daily also said Moellemann had been speaking after meeting Iranian Minister of Mines and Metals Mohammad Hossein Mahlouji in Tehran on Sunday.

"I emphasise the need for restoring diplomatic and economic relations between Iran and Germany," Moellemann was quoted as saying. The newspaper said the officials had discussed cooperation in the field of mines and metals.

The German Embassy in Tehran said Moellemann had been in Tehran for talks. "He was here and held technical discussions, (talks) about projects," a German embassy spokesman in Tehran said, without giving further details on the trip.
The paper quoted Mahlouji as saying Tehran wanted good ties with Germany, but it was up to Bonn to make the first move.
"The politicians in Bonn should take the initiative to restore relations and Tehran is interested in having good relations with Germany and Europe," he was quoted as saying.

But a German Foreign Ministry spokesman in Bonn said Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel had recently made it clear it was up to Tehran to make the first move by showing Bonn the German ambassador to Tehran was welcome to come back.

He said Kinkel had been cautiously optimistic about an improvement in relations after the new Iranian president Mohammad Khatami comes to power. "It is Tehran's turn now," the ministry spokesman told a regular news conference in Bonn.

European Union states except for Greece recalled their ambassadors from Tehran after the court ruled that Iranian leaders ordered the 1992 killings of Kurdish dissidents in Germany. Iran has repeatedly denied involvement.
While the EU later agreed that the ambassadors could return to Tehran, the bloc has suspended ministerial ties as well as its "critical dialogue" with Iran.
Under the critical dialogue policy, the EU had continued to talk to Iran while trying to get it to move closer to the West.

Radjavi condemned Moelleman in his statement, saying: "Shaking hands with criminal terrorists, who were identified by a Berlin court as being responsible for assassinating dissidents abroad, blatantly contradicts the spirit and letter of decisions reached on April 29 by EU foreign ministers".
The NCR, which has its headquarters in Paris, was referring to a decision to recall EU envoys from Tehran. Bonn's ambassador has still not returned to Tehran.
